procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated with a detention order passed by the respondents (likely an administrative or law enforcement body).
procedural_history.impugned_order: The Judgment and Order dated 06.10.2023 of the High Court at Calcutta in WPA(H) No.68 of 2023.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The brother-in-law of the detenue filed a Writ Petition (WPA(H) No.68 of 2023) in the High Court of Calcutta challenging the validity of the detention order. The Division Bench of the High Court of Calcutta dismissed the Writ Petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The brother-in-law of the detenue, aggrieved by the High Court's refusal to set aside the detention order, appealed to the Supreme Court in Criminal Appeal No. 45 of 2024. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, finding no ground to interfere with the High Court's order.

directions: Pending application(s), if any, stand(s) disposed of.

issue.issue_text: Validity of the detention order passed by the respondents.

facts: The respondents attempted to serve the grounds of detention, translated into Bengali, on the detenue the day after his detention.
The detenue repeatedly refused to receive the documents, although he was given the opportunity to read them in their entirety.
A 'panchnama' (an official record) was prepared, which the detenue signed in English, adding the note "I have refused to receive any document".
While refusing to accept the documents, the detenue filed a writ petition claiming that the grounds of detention had not been served on him.
The detenue eventually accepted the documents on the third attempt.
law: Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, a detenue has the right to be informed of the grounds for detention and the right to make a representation against it.
If the written grounds of detention inform the detenue of their right to make a representation, there is no mandatory requirement to also inform them verbally.
A verbal communication of this right is only required if the written grounds do not mention it.
application: The Court found that the respondents had fulfilled their duty by attempting to serve the grounds of detention at the earliest opportunity.
The Court concluded that the detenue's refusal to accept the documents was a "deliberate ploy" to create a basis for challenging the detention order.
The evidence showed the detenue had read the documents and was aware of his rights, as confirmed by the panchnama which he signed and annotated in English.
By reading the documents, the detenue was made aware of his right to make a representation, satisfying the legal requirement.
The Court determined that the detenue had approached the court with "unclean hands" by suppressing the fact that he had refused to receive the documents after reading them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the detention order, finding it valid. The Court held that the detenue was properly informed of the grounds for his detention and his right to representation, but he deliberately refused to accept the documents as a ploy to challenge the order. Since the authorities followed the correct procedure and the detenue was aware of his rights, there was no reason to invalidate the detention.

issue.issue_text: Whether the communication regarding the detenue's right to make a representation must be made both orally and in writing.

facts: The appellant argued that the detenue was not informed of his right to make a representation against the detention order.
The authorities attempted to serve the written grounds of detention to the detenue the day after his detention.
The detenue refused to formally receive the grounds of detention.

Evidence, including a panchnama (an official record of events), showed that the detenue had read the grounds and relevant documents, understood English, and was therefore aware of his right to make a representation.
law: Under Article 22(5) of the Constitution, a detenue must be informed of their right to make a representation against the detention order.
The communication of this right can be either oral or in writing; it is not mandatory for it to be both in every situation.
The primary goal is to ensure the detenue has effective knowledge of their rights, and the method of communication must be sufficient to achieve this based on the circumstances.
application: The Court established a situational test. If a detenue receives the written grounds of detention in a language they understand, and those grounds clearly state the right to make a representation, then a separate verbal communication is not necessary.
However, a verbal explanation is required if the written grounds do not mention this right, if the detenue cannot understand the language, or if the detenue refuses to receive the written grounds.
In this case, the court found that even though the detenue refused to formally accept the documents, he had read them and was well aware of his right. His refusal was deemed a "deliberate ploy."
Because the detenue had effective knowledge of his right through reading the documents, the authorities had fulfilled their constitutional duty.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the communication must always be made both orally and in writing. It held that the communication can be either oral or written, depending on the circumstances, as long as it effectively informs the detenue of their right. Since the detenue had read the grounds and was aware of his right, the requirement was met.

arguments.issue_text: Validity of the detention order passed by the respondents.
appellant_arguments: The detenue was not informed of his constitutional right to make a representation against the detention order.
Not all relevant materials, such as telephonic conversations, were served on the detenue.
The respondents failed to obtain an affidavit from the concerned official regarding the detenue's alleged refusal to receive the grounds of detention.
The grounds of detention could have been served on the detenue's family members.
It is incorrect to claim that the detenue refused to receive the grounds of detention.
In cases involving detention orders, if two interpretations are possible, the one favoring the detenue should be adopted.
respondent_arguments: Multiple attempts were made to serve the grounds of detention, which the detenue initially refused to receive.
The detenue filed a writ petition claiming non-service of the grounds on the very day he refused to accept them for the second time, indicating he approached the court with 'unclean hands'.
The procedure was duly followed; documents were translated into Bengali, and a panchnama was signed by independent witnesses documenting the refusal.
The detenue eventually read the grounds of detention and the relevant documents, making him fully aware of his rights.
The detenue's actions were a 'deliberate ploy' to secure a favorable court order by suppressing facts.
The panchnama, which the detenue signed and annotated in English, demonstrates his proficiency in the language and awareness of the proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the communication regarding the detenue's right to make a representation must be made both orally and in writing.
appellant_arguments: The detenue was not communicated his right to make a representation, which is a mandatory requirement under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.
Mere service of documents in English is insufficient if the detenue does not understand the language well enough to make an effective representation.
An oral explanation by a police officer does not constitute effective communication of the grounds; the detenue must be given effective knowledge of the facts and circumstances.
respondent_arguments: There is no need for a separate verbal communication of the right to representation if the written grounds of detention already contain this information.
A verbal explanation is only required when the written grounds of detention do not mention the right to make a representation.
In this case, the grounds of detention were made known to the detenue, and he read them, which is sufficient communication.
The detenue was well aware of his right to make a representation after reading the documents provided.

cases.case_name: Lallubhai Jogibhai Patel v. Union of India
cases.principle: Cited to reinforce the court's exposition of the law regarding the two-fold obligation on the detaining authority under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: State of Bombay v. Atma Ram Shridhar Vaidya
cases.principle: Cited for the principle that Article 22(5) contains two distinct but correlated rights: 1) the right to be furnished with the grounds for detention, and 2) the right to make a representation against the detention, for which a detenu can ask for further particulars if the initial grounds are insufficient. An infringement of either right allows the detenu to approach the court.
Cited to reinforce the court's exposition of the law regarding the two-fold obligation on the detaining authority under Article 22(5) of the Constitution.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a detenue consciously declines to receive the grounds of detention, the detaining authority is still obligated to inform the detenue of their right to make a representation against the detention order.
obiter: In a case where a detenue is not in a position to understand the language, a mere verbal explanation would not suffice.

If a detenue receives the grounds of detention in a language known to them, and those grounds contain a clear statement of their right to make a representation, there is no need for an additional verbal notification of that right.

The right to be furnished with grounds for detention and the right to make a representation are two distinct rights; the test for the sufficiency of the grounds is different for satisfying the detaining authority versus enabling the detained person to make a representation.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that the two rights granted under Article 22(5) of the Constitution—the right to be furnished with the grounds for detention and the right to be afforded the earliest opportunity to make a representation—are distinct and not a single, indivisible right. The authorities fulfilled their constitutional duty by attempting to serve the grounds of detention at the earliest opportunity, and the other grounds raised by the appellant did not merit acceptance.
legal_tests_applied: Article 22(5) of the Constitution creates two distinct rights: 1) the right to be furnished with the grounds of the detention order 'as soon as may be', and 2) the right to be afforded the 'earliest opportunity' of making a representation against the order. To treat these two rights as one is improper according to the language and purpose of the Article.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's argument that the two rights under Article 22(5) are an indivisible whole, stating, 'We are unable to read Art. 22(5) in that way... the use of the words “as soon as may be” with the obligation to furnish the grounds of the order of detention, and the fixing of another time limit, viz., the earliest opportunity, for making the representation, makes the two rights distinct.'

The court made a factual finding that the authorities had complied with their procedural obligations, stating, 'We also find that the grounds of detention were attempted to be served on the detenue at the earliest point of time – i.e. on the very next day after his detention.'
The court dismissed the appellant's other arguments as unpersuasive, concluding, 'The other grounds raised also do not merit any acceptance, in the light of our earlier discussion.'
why_respondent_won: The court's interpretation of Article 22(5) as creating two separate rights validated the respondent's actions. The court relied on precedent which held, 'To treat the two rights mentioned in Art. 22(5) as one is neither proper according to the language used, nor according to the purpose for which the rights are given.'

The court accepted the respondent's factual claim that they had fulfilled their duty by promptly attempting to serve the detention grounds, which is the first of the two distinct rights under Article 22(5).
policy_considerations: The purpose of furnishing grounds for detention is to enable the detenue to make a representation, giving them an opportunity to present objections against the order. This procedural right is fulfilled when the government provides the grounds, which are the conclusions upon which its satisfaction is based.
